A '''function''' is a many(one)-to-one map between two [[set|sets]]. 

== Formal definition ==

Let $D_f,C_f,R_f \neq \emptyset$ be [[set|sets]].

If

$$
\forall x \in D_f: \exists y \in C_f, f(x)=y,
$$

then $f$ is a function of '''domain''' $D_f$ and '''codomain''' $C_f$, noted as $f: D_f \to C_f$;

Furthermore,

if 

$$
\forall y \in R_f \subseteq C_f, \exists x \in D_f, f(x)=y,
$$

then $R_f$ is the '''range''' of $f$;

Lastly,

if 

$$
\exists f^{-1} : \forall y \in R_f, f^{-1}(y)=x,
$$

then function $f$ is said to be '''invertible''' and the '''bijection''' of $D$ to $R_f$. $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are said to be '''inverse functions''' of each other.

<blockquote>
While a function can be many-to-one, a bijection is an one-to-one function of its domain to its range.
</blockquote>

{{Hidden example}}
$$
f(x)=2x^2, x \in \mathbb{R}
$$

is a function, where $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$.

It is however not a bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$, as $\exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \nexists f^{-1}, f^{-1}(y)=x$, such as $y=-1$

<blockquote>
Note the range $R_f \subset \mathbb{R}$, as $\exists y \in \mathbb{R}: y \notin R_f$, such as $y=-1$
</blockquote>

<ref>{{#cite:Q2199}}</ref>
{{End hidden}}

== Image and preimage ==

Given function $f: A \to B$

If for $A_1 \subseteq A, B_1 \subseteq B$,

$$
B_1=f(A_1)=\{f(a)|\forall a \in A_1\}
$$

Then $B_1$ is known as the '''image''' of $A_1$ in $B$ under $f$, and $A_1$ is known as the '''pre-image''' of $B_1$ under $f$, noted $f^{\leftarrow}(B_1)=A_1$

<ref>{{#cite:Q2199}}</ref>

== Composition ==

Let $f,g$ be functions:

$$
f: A \to B \\
g: C \to D
$$

where $A,B,C,D$ are sets

If $B \subseteq C$, then is defined the composite function

$$
g \circ f: A \to D
$$
where $\forall x \in A$, $g\circ f (x)=g(f(x))$

== Properties ==

=== $f^{-1}[f(x)]=x; f[f^{-1}(y)]=y$ ===

Given for arbitrary function $f: D \to R$

$$
\exists f^{-1}: R \to D \\
x \in D, y \in R
$$

{{Hidden proof}}

By [[#Formal_definition|definition]],

$$
\forall x \in D: \exists y \in R,\, f(x)=y
$$

By [[#Formal_definition|definition]],

$$
f^{-1}(y)=x \\
\therefore f^{-1}[f(x)]=f^{-1}(y)=x
$$

Let $g=f^{-1}$, then $g^{-1}=f$. Since $f$ is an arbitrary function, $g$ is also an arbitrary function where

$$
g[g^{-1}(y)]=g(x)=y
$$

Hence

$$
f^{-1}[f(x)]=x; f[f^{-1}(y)]=y
$$
{{End hidden}}
